For production containers, by default use an appropriate runtime image rather
than the SDK image solely for convenience, and do not switch to root merely to
bypass filesystem permission problems.

Keep build tooling out of production runtime images, keep images reproducible
and configuration external, keep Docker concerns separate from application
architecture, and use the deployment platform's health-probe capabilities when
practical.

Use a multi-stage build:

Use the ASP.NET runtime image for ASP.NET Core applications and an appropriate
.NET runtime image for workers that do not require ASP.NET Core.

Use the built-in non-root user of modern .NET images when it fits the image and
deployment environment (`USER app`), and give directories the application
writes to appropriate ownership and permissions.

Start with standard supported .NET runtime images. Consider Alpine, chiseled
images, trimming, Native AOT, or other size optimizations only when
compatibility and deployment requirements justify them, and verify
globalization, native dependencies, reflection, and diagnostics when using
specialized images.

The Microsoft resilience packages build on Polly v8, but application code uses

## Hedging

Hedging issues parallel or delayed duplicate attempts. Use it only for
operations that are safe to execute multiple times, typically idempotent reads
against interchangeable endpoints; do not hedge state-changing operations.

## Database Resilience

Do not wrap normal persistence operations in a generic application-level retry
pipeline. When the persistence provider supports transient retry through its
execution strategy or provider configuration, prefer that mechanism, and handle
transaction/retry interaction according to the provider's guidance (persistence
knowledge skill). An HTTP retry policy is not automatically appropriate for
database operations.

Check-by-reference against the policy owners above: string interpolation in
structured logs; duplicate exception logging; expected business outcomes logged
as errors; credentials or secrets logged; full objects dumped without review;
provider-specific APIs spread through Application code; logs used as an audit
database without a dedicated audit design.

- Use two-stage initialization when startup logging matters: a bootstrap logger
  captures failures before the full DI/configuration pipeline exists. Simpler
  applications may use normal host-managed Serilog setup without bootstrap
  logging.
- Register with `builder.Services.AddSerilog()`, which integrates with DI
  services through `ReadFrom.Services(services)`, rather than the older
  `builder.Host.UseSerilog()`.
- Message templates (`{PropertyName}`) create queryable structured data; string
  interpolation breaks structure and allocates even when the level is disabled.
- Keep log levels, sinks, and overrides in `appsettings` so they can vary per
  environment without redeployment.
- Keep direct Serilog APIs such as `Log.Logger` and `LogContext` at composition
  or provider-specific boundaries.

## Elasticsearch Sink

The `Serilog.Sinks.Elasticsearch` package is deprecated; use the official
`Elastic.Serilog.Sinks` package, which writes ECS-formatted documents to data
streams:

| Scenario | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Serilog as provider | `AddSerilog()` + configuration |
| General application logging API | `ILogger<T>` (logging skill) |
| Log storage (development) | Seq (free single-user) or Aspire Dashboard |
| Log storage (production) | Seq, Elasticsearch (Elastic sink), or an OTLP backend |
| Request logging | `UseSerilogRequestLogging()` |
| Scoped properties | `LogContext.PushProperty()` in middleware |
| Log filtering | `Serilog.Expressions` |
| High-performance paths | `[LoggerMessage]` source generator |
| Audit trails | `AuditTo` (synchronous, exceptions propagate) |
| Log levels by environment | `MinimumLevel.Override` per namespace in appsettings |
| OpenTelemetry integration | `Serilog.Sinks.OpenTelemetry` (no SDK dependency) |

explicit request and use-case validation.
